title: Core SQL, Joins, NULL Traps & Fundamental Logic
notes: Key written for the question paper (the supplied key was for other questions). Every query and statement below is run on MySQL, MariaDB and PostgreSQL with the practice data by run.py --verify-key; theory answers are graded by must-have facts (each inner list = one fact, any of its words).

questions.ref: SELECT first_name, last_name, salary FROM employees WHERE dept_id IN (10, 30) AND salary >= 55000 ORDER BY hire_date DESC
SELECT emp_id, first_name FROM employees WHERE dept_id IS NULL
SELECT salary FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL ORDER BY salary ASC LIMIT 5

questions.proof: SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(b), AVG(b) FROM (SELECT 100 AS b UNION ALL SELECT NULL UNION ALL SELECT 200 UNION ALL SELECT NULL UNION ALL SELECT 300) t

questions.ref: UPDATE employees SET salary = salary * 1.08 WHERE hire_date < '2024-01-01'
questions.state: SELECT emp_id, salary FROM employees ORDER BY emp_id

questions.ref: SELECT DISTINCT UPPER(location) AS location FROM departments
SELECT emp_id, salary FROM employees WHERE (dept_id = 10 OR dept_id = 20) AND salary > 60000 ORDER BY salary DESC
SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(e.emp_id) AS employee_count FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name
SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(e.emp_id) FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id AND e.salary > 50000 GROUP BY d.dept_name

questions.proof_note: MariaDB has no FULL OUTER JOIN either (the supplied key said 10.5 added it; it did not).

questions.ref: SELECT e.first_name AS employee, m.first_name AS manager FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.emp_id = e.manager_id
SELECT e.first_name FROM employees e WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employees m WHERE m.manager_id = e.emp_id)
SELECT d.dept_name, AVG(e.salary) FROM departments d JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name HAVING AVG(e.salary) > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees)
SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS occurrences FROM employees GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
SELECT band, COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT CASE WHEN salary >= 80000 THEN 'High' ELSE 'Low' END AS band FROM employees) t WHERE band = 'High' GROUP BY band
SELECT d.dept_name FROM departments d WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM projects p WHERE p.dept_id = d.dept_id AND p.status = 'active')

questions.ref_mysql: UPDATE employees e JOIN (SELECT MAX(salary) AS mx, MIN(salary) AS mn FROM employees) s ON e.salary IN (s.mx, s.mn) SET e.salary = CASE WHEN e.salary = s.mx THEN s.mn ELSE s.mx END
questions.ref_postgres: UPDATE employees SET salary = CASE WHEN salary = (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees) THEN (SELECT MIN(salary) FROM employees) ELSE (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees) END WHERE salary IN ((SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees), (SELECT MIN(salary) FROM employees))
questions.state: SELECT emp_id, salary FROM employees ORDER BY emp_id

questions.ref: SELECT d1.dept_id, d1.salary FROM (SELECT DISTINCT dept_id, salary FROM employees) d1 WHERE 2 = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT e2.salary) FROM employees e2 WHERE e2.dept_id = d1.dept_id AND e2.salary > d1.salary)
SELECT d.dept_name, MAX(e.salary) AS max_salary FROM departments d JOIN employees e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id GROUP BY d.dept_name
SELECT e.first_name FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON m.emp_id = e.manager_id WHERE e.salary > m.salary AND e.hire_date < m.hire_date
